Important Figures

This reference page identifies historical figures connected to key shifts in telescope design, observation, and astronomical method.

Hans Lipperhey

Lipperhey's 1608 lens-based instrument is the earliest documented evidence of the telescope in practical use, initiating instrument-assisted observation.

Galileo

Galileo used telescopic observation to report lunar relief, Jovian moons, and dense star fields, providing evidence that challenged inherited cosmological claims.

Thomas Harriot

Harriot produced early telescopic drawings of the Moon in 1609, documenting surface variation with map-like attention to light and shadow.

Kepler

Kepler described a convex-eyepiece refracting configuration that expanded magnification options and influenced later standard telescope design.

Newton

Newton's reflecting telescope demonstrated how mirrors could reduce chromatic aberration, establishing a durable alternative to long refractors.

Elisabetha Hevelius

Elisabetha Hevelius contributed directly to observation, recording, and publication work, illustrating the collaborative labor behind early modern astronomy.

Caroline Herschel

Caroline Herschel advanced observational astronomy through systematic surveys and comet discovery, showing the value of disciplined long-term observing practice.

Edwin Hubble

Edwin Hubble helped establish the extragalactic scale of the universe and provided observational evidence for cosmic expansion, framing modern cosmology.
